Avery / team — quick working draft recommendation below. Attaching a short PDF with the SKU breakout (redwood_proposed_sku_breakdown.pdf). High-level first-pass guidance:

Summary recommendation (short): hybrid committed pool with A100s as the backbone + targeted H100 slots for long-context, latency-sensitive tails, and L4s for low-cost embedding throughput. Rough ratio: 60% A100 / 20% H100 / 20% L4 by capacity units (see notes).

Rationale and tradeoffs:
- H100 (best for very long contexts, fp16/fp8 training parity): choose when a single request must keep >128k token KV state or when you run large decoder-only models that exceed A100 memory even when quantized. Pros: highest single-request memory and fastest step throughput for heavy-context decoding. Cons: highest committed cost, less efficient for high-QPS short requests.

- A100 (balanced): strong for moderate-long contexts (up to ~64k tokens depending on model and quantization), excellent for throughput-oriented services. Pros: predictable performance for mixed prompt lengths, cost-effective per-token on steady-state traffic. Cons: can run out of per-model residency memory for extreme context sizes.

- L4 (inference-optimized, quantized): excellent for embeddings and small-chat flows where high parallelism reduces per-token cost. Pros: very low cost per token for quantized models, dense packing for high-QPS embedding batches. Cons: limited memory for long contexts; may require model slicing or shorter context windows.

Sizing sketch (based on your numbers):
- Steady state 18 req/sec (avg 1.9k tokens total): A100 pool sized to cover steady-state and 75% of typical peaks: ~6 A100 nodes (example: 40 TFLOPS-equivalent nodes; translate to capacity units in the attached PDF).
- Peak headroom: allow burst to cover spikes up to 180 req/sec — recommend 12 L4 nodes for fast-burst parallelism + 4 H100 minutes-equivalent slots to cover p99 tail when requests are long and cannot be sharded.
- Embedding batch: run on L4 dense pool during night; estimate 8–10 L4 nodes for an 8-hour window to finish 4M records, or move to burst-scheduled cloud instances if you want to exclude from committed base.

Operational notes and fallbacks:
- Use automatic prefix KV caching to reduce upstream compute for repeated contexts (saves 10–35% tokens depending on reuse).
- Canary route long-context requests to H100 set, short-chat to A100/L4 to reduce p99 latency exposure.
- If committed spend is constrained, recommend committing fewer H100 slots and using on-demand burst for short-term heavy tails. We can model cost impact in the deck.

Cost sensitivity: switching 1 H100 for 4 A100-equivalent instances reduces peak committed cost but increases risk of hitting memory limits on single requests. L4s lower per-token costs for embedding workloads by ~3–6x vs A100 depending on quant.

Open items for sizing accuracy:
- exact model binaries and quantization format (int8, q4/q8) which change memory footprint drastically
- expected per-request concurrency distribution (we assumed Poisson with short tail)

I'll update the PDF with per-node throughput curves and a recommended reserve/burst plan after the sync.

Extra infra/ops context to consider before finalizing commits:

1) Node packing and memory fragmentation:
- A100 and H100 memory semantics differ; some model runtimes reserve contiguous memory for KV caches. If Zebra's model keeps large KV per-request, we must account for fragmentation and reduce effective capacity by ~8–12%.

2) Autoscaling and burst choreography:
- Put L4s in a high-density burst pool (fast spin-up). Configure autoscaler with request-based policy + token backlog thresholds instead of pure CPU/GPU utilization to avoid latency-blind scale-ups.

3) KV cache eviction and cross-model residency:
- If you want strict no off-host caching, use pinned-residency scheduling for a subset of H100s and A100s (reserve 2–3 nodes for hot sessions). This increases reserved cost but protects p99 latency.

4) Reliability and fallthrough policy:
- Recommend canarying a 5% traffic route to L4-backed quantized model variants first. On failure, route to A100; only route to H100 when memory constraints force it. This keeps most traffic on lower-cost hardware.

5) Billing and reporting implications:
- We'll provide token-level cost attribution. If embeddings are run on burst on-demand instances, they should be separated in billing to avoid committed overage disputes.

I'll also push a short ops checklist with specific autoscaler thresholds and reservation counts.
